statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#cor:cd-remaining
Only CD∈{−2,−1} remain among the exceptional dyadic cells

At a final middle row D≥13, Theorem 10.6 removes −3 from the exceptional set {−3,−2,−1}, leaving −2,−1 within that set. It does not assert CD∈{−2,−1}: nonnegative values have not been excluded. statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#cor:mersenne-height
Mersenne specialisation

Let x be a positive rational number and let r≥0, n≥1 be integers. If 2r∣x.num.natAbs and x<2/(2n−1), then 2r⋅(2n−1)<2⋅x.den ; a numerator 2-power lower bound plus a Mersenne-scale upper bound on x together force a denominator lower bound, without introducing a global prefix LCM. To see the inequality directly, write x=a/b in lowest terms with a,b>0. The hypotheses give a≥2r and a(2n−1)<2b. The conclusion follows by substitution. An application of Lemma 10.13 must in addition supply its denominator-divisibility assumptions.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#cor:negative-mobius-overshoot
Negative-Möbius Boolean support overshoots 1/2

Let N={d≥2:μ(d)=−1}. Isolating the d=1 term in Theorem 6.28 gives

XN(2)=12+∑d≥2μ(d)=112d−1≥12+163>12,

since μ(6)=1. This rules out the particular candidate N. It does not rule out other infinite supports representing 1/2.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#cor:tr-half-lcm
Half-LCM horizon
Let J≥2 and LJ:=lcm(2,3,…,J). For every n≥max{4,LJ/2+1} there is an M∈[n,2n−2] with μJ(M)<11/15. Thus witness exclusion leaves only the finite window [4,LJ/2] to check.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:collapse-mech
Carry and residual value

Let A⊆ℕ with 1∉A, put δ:=1/2−xA, and let ihc⁡(A,N) denote the integer half-carry at level N. Then

ihc⁡(A,N)=2N+1δ+T(N+1),0≤T(N+1)≤2N+1+4,

where T(m)=∑r≥1cA(m+r)2−r.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:denominator-sandwich

The odd denominator survives dyadic
subtraction

Let r/D be a reduced fraction with D>0 odd, let p∈ℤ, and let c≥0 be an integer. The reduced denominator of p/2c−r/D is divisible by D and divides 2cD. Indeed, its unreduced numerator pD−2cr is coprime to D, since gcd(r,D)=gcd(2c,D)=1. Reduction can therefore remove only powers of 2 from the displayed denominator. No property of Mersenne weights is used.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:denominator-survival

A guaranteed divisor of a reduced
denominator

Let a∈ℤ, D∈ℕ>0 and m,C,h∈ℕ. Write den⁡(x) for the positive reduced denominator of a rational number x. If m∣D and gcd(m,|a|)=1, then m∣den⁡(a/D). If C∣D and gcd(C,|a|)=1, then

Cgcd(C,h)∣den⁡(ha/D).

Thus scaling may remove part of the guaranteed divisor. Indeed, reduction divides D by gcd(D,|a|), so no prime power in m can be lost. After scaling, a prime p∣C can lose at most vp(h) powers from the guaranteed divisor. This is a lower bound on the reduced denominator, not an equality: for D=12, C=6, a=1, h=2, it guarantees the divisor 3, while the reduced denominator is 6. The lemma feeds Theorem 6.24 directly.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:dyadic-excess-reformulation

An integer test for the interval between
the dyadic and Mersenne weights

For positive integers p,L and n≥0, write the residual as p/(2L) and put E=2np−L. Clearing positive denominators gives

p2L≤12n+1⟺E≤0,12n+1<p2L<12n+1−1⟺0<E<p2.

The first test concerns the dyadic bound, not the greedy selection threshold itself. The second identifies precisely the interval in which a Mersenne weight is skipped but the dyadic safety test fails.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:eventually-right-impossible

The values on either side of an eventual
right continuation

If the seam eventually always extends “true” (right branch) from some row S on with a fixed lower prefix u, the resulting cofinite-support value stays strictly below 1/2; the matching alternative “upper competitor” word gives a strict excess above 1/2. Neither of these two cofinite continuations represents 1/2. This does not rule out an eventually-right integer orbit; it describes the two values in that case. The inequalities are used in Theorem 6.44.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:fatal-gap-exclusion

A greedy gap excludes every
representation

Let d≥0 be an integer and u⊆{1,…,d} a finite prefix. If

Xu(2)+Rd+1<t<Xu(2)+wd+1,

then no support agreeing with u through rank d represents t: omitting d+1 leaves value at most the lower endpoint, while including it gives value at least the upper endpoint. Other length-d prefixes have disjoint containing intervals by the first-difference argument using wn>Rn. Since the displayed gap lies inside the interval for u, none of those prefixes can represent t either. Thus a certified strict gap excludes every representation, not just one proposed continuation.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:gap-mass-summability
Summability of one gap length per level

For n≥1, put gn=wn−Rn>0. The sum of one gap length per level satisfies, for N≥0,

∑n>Ngn≤294−N+378−N.

This follows by summing the per-level upper bounds geometrically. It is not the measure of the union of all gaps: level n has 2n−1 translated gaps of length gn. The corresponding weighted sum and its geometric interpretation are given after Theorem 6.118. Neither estimate decides membership of a specified point such as 1/2.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:half-divisor-unit-drop
The effect of adding one divisor

Let N≥0 and let finite supports D0,D1 differ only by D1=D0∪{N+1}, with N+1∉D0. For every positive integer m,

cD1(m)−cD0(m)=𝟏N+1∣m.

In particular, the difference is 1 at m=2(N+1). This follows directly from the definition of a divisor count. Its use in another coefficient sequence requires proving that sequence has the same support-incidence description.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:half-endpoint-kills
No finite Mersenne sum equals one half

For every finite u⊆ℕ>0, Xu(2)≠1/2: its reduced denominator is odd. Also Xu(2)+Rd≠1/2 for every d≥0, since Rd is the irrational full Mersenne sum minus a finite rational sum. These observations exclude equality at the finite-prefix and complete-tail endpoints of Lemma 6.36.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:largest-false-rank-algebra

The exact gap at the largest omitted
rank

Let 2≤d<s and 2s<3d. Write Ws(E)=∑e∈E⌊4s/(2e−1)⌋ for a finite set E⊆{2,…,s−1}. For u⊆{2,…,d−1}, put E−=u∪{d+1,…,s−1} and E+=u∪{d}. Then

3Ws(E−)+3⋅2s+1+2⋅4s−d+4=3Ws(E+).

The correction is independent of the common prefix u. For the integer-greedy rows s≥5, a right transition preserves the largest omitted rank, whereas an upper or middle transition makes s the largest omitted rank in the next row.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:linear-channel-nogo

Linear functionals factoring through one
value

Let V be a vector space over ℚ, let ev:V→ℚ be linear, and choose e∈V with ev(e)=1. Suppose that each linear functional ℓj:V→ℚ vanishes on ker⁡(ev). Then v−ev(v)e∈ker⁡(ev) gives ℓj(v)=ℓj(e)ev(v). Consequently any finite evaluation matrix (ℓj(vi))i,j is an outer product and has rank at most one. Every square minor of order at least two therefore vanishes. This excludes determinant arguments formed from these particular functionals, not determinant methods with additional independent information.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:mersenne-tail-weight

Each Mersenne weight exceeds its remaining
tail

For n≥1, let wn=(2n−1)−1 and Rn=∑j>nwj. Then

Rn=wn+1+Rn+1,2−n<Rn≤2wn+1<wn.

For the upper bound, compare each tail term with 21−jwn+1 at index n+j, j≥1, and sum the geometric series. The last inequality follows by comparing 2/(2n+1−1) with 1/(2n−1). This strict term-versus-tail inequality is the separation hypothesis used in the greedy arguments.

It is not available for the totient weights φ(n)/2n: the terms at indices 4 and 5 already sum to 2/16+4/32=1/4=φ(3)/23, and the remaining tail is positive. A general strict-tail argument therefore cannot be transferred to that sequence without a different hypothesis or proof.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:mixed-prime-power-layer
Commuting prime-power differences

For a function g:ℕ>0→ℤ, a positive integer p and an integer e≥1, define

(Δp,eg)(n)=g(pen)−g(pe−1n).

These operators commute. If p≠q are primes, e,f≥1, A⊆ℕ>0, n≥1 and gcd(n,pq)=1, then

(Δq,fΔp,ecA)(n)=∑d∣n𝟏A(peqfd).

Thus the mixed difference counts precisely the support elements whose p- and q-adic exponents are e and f in this divisor sum.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:no-ties
No-ties lemma
At every rank k of the full greedy orbit for target 1/2, both defining comparisons are strict: ρ≠xk and ρ≠Tk+1.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:odometer

Divisor-residue form of the short-window
phase

For all M,L≥1,

ΘL(M) = ∑d≥2 ∑1≤i≤Li≡−M (mod d)2−i = ∑d≥2 2−id(M)⋅1−2−dmd1−2−d,

where id(M)∈[1,d] is the least i≥1 with d∣M+i (so id(M) depends only on Mmodd), md:=#{1≤i≤L:d∣M+i}, and terms with id(M)>L are empty. In particular, for every integer D≥M+L,

ΘL(M) = ∑d=2D ∑i=1L2−i𝟏d∣M+i,

and the right-hand side, with an arbitrary integer x≥0 in place of M, depends on x only through its residues modulo the integers d with 2≤d≤D. The cutoff D has to be fixed before the argument varies: at (M,L)=(1,1) the cutoff is M+L=2, the integers 1 and 3 have the same residue modulo every d with 2≤d≤2, and yet Θ1(1)=1/2 while Θ1(3)=1.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:rank-step-trichotomy

The two next-prefix intervals and their
gap

Let d≥0 be an integer, let u⊆{1,…,d}, and suppose the target t lies in the interval [Xu(2),Xu(2)+Rd]. At depth d+1, either t lies in the lower interval

[Xu(2),Xu(2)+Rd+1],

or in the upper interval

[Xu(2)+wd+1,Xu(2)+wd+1+Rd+1],

or in the open gap between them. These alternatives are disjoint because Rd+1<wd+1, and exhaustive because Rd=wd+1+Rd+1. For t=1/2, Lemma 6.38 also excludes the interval endpoints, so all relevant comparisons are strict. Endpoint exclusion is not what makes the two child intervals disjoint; the strict-tail inequality does that.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:reverse-carry-word
Spacing of reverse-carry words

For i=1,2, let integer sequences ai,bi,ui satisfy

bi(m)+2ui(m)=ai(m)+ui(m+1).

Let k,L≥0 be integers. Suppose that at index k the coefficients agree and b1(k)−b2(k)=1. Suppose also that both coefficients and bits agree at indices k+1,…,k+L. Then

u1(k+L+1)−u2(k+L+1)=2L(2(u1(k)−u2(k))+1).

The factor in parentheses is an odd integer. If the two terminal carries have absolute values at most B1,B2, respectively, then 2L≤B1+B2. For a common bound B the conclusion is 2L≤2B, not 2L≤B. The formula follows by subtracting the two recurrences: the initial bit difference gives the odd factor, and each subsequent agreement doubles it. An application must supply the stated agreements and terminal bounds.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:scalar-localization
Denominator complement survives scaling

For x:ℚ, c:ℤ, H:ℕ: if H∣x.den and (c⋅x).den∣H ; i.e. multiplying by the integer c shrinks the displayed denominator down into H ; then the complementary denominator factor x.den/H divides c:

H∣x.den ∧ (c⋅x).den∣H⟹x.den/H∣|c|.

Equivalently, writing D=x.den/H, we have D∣c, so t=c/D is an integer and Hcx=tx.num. Here H>0 follows from H∣x.den, since the reduced denominator is positive.

Scope. This is elementary rational arithmetic, independent of the problem. If c≠0, divisibility gives the size bound |c|≥x.den/H. The nonzero condition is essential: c=0 clears every denominator and satisfies the divisibility conclusion without any positive lower bound on |c|. The lemma therefore constrains denominator clearing by a nonzero bounded multiplier, not arbitrary multiplication. Object or representation: about a representation ; pure denominator bookkeeping for ℚ, with zero problem-specific content; the upstream primitive is the domain-neutral extraction this lemma builds on.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:seam-upper-or-middle
Seam upper-or-middle classification

At a row s≥5, the terminal rank is omitted in the next row, s∉Ds+1, if and only if either

4os+ps+≤2s+1,

or this inequality fails and

4rem(s)+2s+1−ps−<2s+2+4.

These are exactly branches U and M of Theorem 5.16. On either branch the new terminal weight does not fit; on R it does. This is an exact classification, not a conjecture inferred from observed branch labels.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:skipped-endpoint-trichotomy

The signed position of a skipped greedy
prefix

Let s≥5 be omitted by the real greedy support G, and put

Hs=G∩{2,…,s−1},fs=∑d∈Hs⌊4s2d−1⌋−Ts.

Exactly one of the following holds:

fs<0:Hs=Ds,fs=−rem(s),rem(s)≥1;fs=0:Hs=Ds,rem(s)=0;fs>0:Hs=Bs,fs=os.

Thus the real greedy prefix is one of the two adjacent integer words. This classifies its signed distance fs from Ts; it does not exclude the negative case. Nor does it identify fs with the different coordinate Cs=4rem(s)−ps−−4 used in the final-middle argument.

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:straddle-agrees-greedy

Straddle words are canonical: they agree
with the greedy prefix

Let u⊆{1,…,d} satisfy Xu(2)≤1/2≤Xu(2)+Rd. Then

u=G∩{1,…,d},

where G is the real greedy support for 1/2. At the first disagreement, if u takes rank k and the greedy rule skips it, then Xu(2)>1/2. In the opposite case, the greedy remainder before k is at least wk, whereas the remaining contribution allowed by u, including Rd, is at most Rk<wk. Both cases contradict the displayed interval. Thus there is at most one such word at each depth; the lemma does not assert its existence at every depth.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:tail-transfer
Changing finitely many support elements

Let b≥2 be an integer, and let A,B⊆ℕ≥1. If XA(b) is irrational and A,B have finite symmetric difference, then XB(b) is irrational too: the two sums differ by a finite sum of rational numbers. This observation supplies the finite modifications in Theorem 6.21.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:tr-forced-greedy
Forced greedy

For every J≥2: wn(J)>Tn+1(J) for all n (the q=1 terms agree exactly, and every q≥2 tail term is strictly smaller than the corresponding weight term). Consequently the greedy support is the unique candidate support, and HalfRung(J) holds iff the greedy orbit for 1/2 under weights wn(J) never lands in a fatal interval (Tn+1(J),wn(J)). Rank 1 is always a safe skip; ranks 2 and 3 are always takes.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:tr-mod12
Mod-12 filter, J≥7
For J≥7, the inequality μJ(M)≤11/15 implies 12∣M. Thus only multiples of 12 need be tested as witnesses in each interval [n,2n−2]; no potentially uncovered rank is discarded.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#lem:tr-parity
Parity forces infinite support
For every J≥2, no finite A⊆{2,3,…} attains HalfRung(J).

(12)Wb,𝒫(A𝒰)<∞⟺𝒫∩E∈𝒰.

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:2adic-nogo

Centred completion of
fixed-precision 2-adic data

Fix u≥1 and a finite list (vi,ai)0≤i<m, where vi≥0 are integers and the integers ai are odd. For every initial integer e0, there are integers zi,ei+1 such that

ei+1=2ei+2vi(ai+2uzi),|ei+1|≤2vi+u−1(0≤i<m).

Thus one may prescribe the valuation and u bits of the odd unit of each input coefficient while keeping every successor state in its stated centred interval. The initial state is arbitrary.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:achievement-set-topology

Achievement-set topology: compact,
closed, perfect, measure exactly one

𝒜 is compact (continuous image of the binary-sequence Cantor space ℕ→Fin2 under the product topology, via the positive-index digit map), hence closed; it is also perfect, totally disconnected, and nowhere dense, with Lebesgue measure exactly 1. The compactness/closedness argument (binary coding → Cantor space → continuous image) is a fully generic technique for characterizing the achievement set of any absolutely convergent digit-weighted series, not specific to Mersenne denominators ; reusable for a φ(n)/2n subsum set after checking summability. No separation of successive weights is needed for compactness or closedness; the stronger topological conclusions require their own hypotheses. Closedness alone is what powers every “limit of a sequence of achieved points is achieved” argument in this catalogue (e.g. Theorem 6.2, Theorem 6.5).
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:canon

Uniqueness under the stated finite
conditions

Put G=greedyMersenneSupport(1/2), wn=(2n−1)−1 and Rd=∑n>dwn. The following are three separate uniqueness statements.

  1. If D⊆{1,…,d} and XD(2)≤1/2≤XD(2)+Rd, then D=G∩{1,…,d}.

  2. If c≥4, D⊆{2,…,c−1} and 0<1/2−XD(2)<wc, then D=G∩{1,…,c−1}.

  3. Let positive integer weights v1,…,vk satisfy vi≥g+∑j>ivj for a positive integer g. For a nonnegative integer target T, let y∗ be the word obtained by visiting these weights in order and taking each when it fits. An admissible Boolean word y has 0≤T−∑iyivi<g if and only if y=y∗ and 0≤T−∑iyi∗vi<g.

Part (iii) gives uniqueness under the small-remainder condition, not existence. Theorem 6.100 gives a one-weight counterexample to dropping that condition.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:carry-survivor-extinction

Period exclusion for the totient
series

For ∑nφ(n)/2n, the cited finite test proves that totientTail(N+h)−totientTail(N) is not an integer by excluding every possible integer state in a bounded range within finitely many steps. If the series were rational, some positive period h0 would make these tail differences integral for every sufficiently large N. Telescoping would then give integrality also for every positive multiple mh0.

Consequently, the required certificate supply is: for every h0≥1 and every lower bound N0, there exist m≥1, N≥N0 and a finite test length K excluding integrality for (mh0,N). The unbounded choice of N is essential; a counterexample before the unknown eventual threshold does not exclude an eventual period. It is sufficient instead to obtain such certificates for h=lcm(1,…,t) with both t and N exceeding arbitrary prescribed lower bounds. The supplied finite theorem excludes the tail differences for 1≤h≤16 at (N,L)=(14,9), and hence excludes rational values whose reduced denominator divides 214(2h−1) for one of those h. It does not establish the unbounded certificate supply.

Scope. The Lean declarations used in this comparison concern the totient series of Problem 249. Their carry recurrences may suggest constructions for Problem 257, but applying them there requires a new argument for the divisor transform of its chosen support. The totient-specific theorems do not supply that argument.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:collapse
A cofinal carry bound
If |ihc⁡(A,N)|≤CN+1+C′ for arbitrarily large N, with fixed constants C,C′, then δ=0. For the particular greedy support A=G of 1/2, a one-sided upper bound ihc⁡(G,N)≤CN+1+C′ already suffices.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:collapsed-list

Six equivalent membership
conditions

Each of the following is logically equivalent to 1/2∈𝒜, not strictly weaker:

  1. CG(N)≤2N+4 for every N≥0;

  2. there are arbitrarily large positive exponents outside G;

  3. at arbitrarily large depths n, some D⊆{2,…,n} satisfies Q(D,n)=2n−1−1; no agreement between the sets D at different depths is required;

  4. at arbitrarily large M, ihc⁡(G,M)≤B(M+1);

  5. at arbitrarily large positive depths M, some D⊆{2,…,M} satisfies |ihc⁡(D,M−1)|≤B(M);

  6. the half-target greedy remainder never exceeds the full remaining tail, so no finite fatal gap exists; the seven equivalent forms in the later classification express this same condition.

For (d) and (e), the reverse directions use the square depths in Lemma 2.6. For (a), membership gives CG(N)≤2N+1+3≤2N+4 when N≥1, and CG(0)=0. The forward implication still needs the greedy inequality xG≤1/2.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:cpgs-equiv

CPGS := ∀N, ∃c≥N, c skipped by the rational half-greedy orbit ∧ 0<r(1/2)(c−1)

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:critical-band-index
Quantifier collapse: one critical index suffices, not d+1

Let d,E∈ℕ and assume E≤2d+1. Then the purely combinatorial statement 𝖣𝗒𝖺𝖽𝗂𝖼𝖡𝖺𝗇𝖽𝖤𝗌𝖼𝖺𝗉𝖾(d,E)⟺∃j, 𝖢𝗋𝗂𝗍𝗂𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖣𝗒𝖺𝖽𝗂𝖼𝖡𝖺𝗇𝖽𝖨𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗑(d,E,j)∧E+2(d+j)≤2d−j+1 collapses the ∀j∈[0,d] band-avoidance condition (formally d+1 separate inequalities) to checking exactly one nearest-boundary index j. The range assumption ensures that a dyadic threshold lies at or above E. Choose the smallest such threshold: smaller thresholds are already below E, while larger thresholds have narrower forbidden bands. Without the range assumption all bands escape automatically when E>2d+1, but no critical index exists; (d,E)=(0,3) is the smallest example. Specialised to the concrete seam reset charge, 𝖲𝖾𝖺𝗆𝖴𝗉𝗉𝖾𝗋𝖱𝖾𝗌𝖾𝗍𝖢𝗋𝗂𝗍𝗂𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖡𝖺𝗇𝖽𝖤𝗌𝖼𝖺𝗉𝖾 is proved logically equivalent to Definition 10.15’s hypothesis. Zero Mersenne/seam content in the core lemma ; pure (d,E,j) arithmetic over powers of 2.

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:exponent-gap

A bound for the reduced
denominator

Let n≥2, let Skipn⊆{2,…,n−1}, and let Dn be the reduced denominator of the associated finite sum. Since Dn divides the product of its Mersenne denominators,

log2⁡Dn≤∑d∈Skipnlog2⁡(2d−1)≤∑d∈Skipnd≤n(n−1)2−1.

The middle inequality is strict when the skip set is nonempty; for an empty skip set both sums are zero. This is an upper bound, not a quadratic asymptotic for Dn. statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:finite-boolSupport-and-onesided

Finite computation and
half-membership

No finite positive-index Boolean support has value exactly 1/2: the reduced denominator of any finite Mersenne subset-sum is provably odd (each 2n−1 is odd), while 1/2 needs an even denominator. Separately, 𝖢𝖾𝗋𝗍𝗂𝖿𝗂𝖾𝖽𝖦𝗋𝖾𝖾𝖽𝗒𝖬𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝗇𝗇𝖾𝖣𝖾𝖺𝗍𝗁 is a finite-depth certificate of x∉𝒜, obtained by decidable tests on rational input. For example, the supplied source excludes 3/4 at level 1 with lookahead 0. Failure to find such a certificate at a given depth does not establish membership. It records survival of that finite test, not survival at every depth.

Scope. Any support representing 1/2, if it exists, must be infinite. This follows from denominator parity, independently of the certificate search. The search supplies a different fact: a successful exclusion certificate proves nonmembership, whereas its absence in a bounded search does not prove membership or rationality. The same distinction must be checked separately for any other certificate family.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:finite-state-nogo

A finite-state restriction for the
stated pulse family

For a “balanced pulse” family at location m≥2 (radius ρ=⌊(m+1)/2⌋, parameters 0≤r≤ρ, moving mass between positions m and m+1 with the weighted total 2c(m)+c(m+1)=2ρ of the two coefficients fixed), if a predecessor state is constant across the whole family, then no function decode:State→ℕ can recover the parameter r from state(r) for every r. The family has exactly ρ+1=⌊(m+1)/2⌋+1 members, so the fan-out is unbounded in m. More strongly, any finite set of states carrying an exact decoder for the family has at least ρ+1 elements, unbounded in m.

Scope. Excludes bounded-state encodings of pre-m history that must distinguish every member of the displayed balanced-pulse family, whether the coefficients are φ or a Möbius-support indicator. Applying it to #249 or #257 requires showing that the relevant orbit realises that family, and it does not rule out every finite-state proof strategy. Object or representation: about a representation class, the encodings of history that separate the balanced-pulse family; it says nothing about C or 𝒜 directly.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#prop:local-void

Limits of the specified local
summaries

(i) After L common steps the endpoint residue mod 2L of an affine binary orbit is independent of the initial carry: u(L)−v(L)=2L(u0−v0). (ii) Fix m≥2 and put h=⌊(m+1)/2⌋. Consider the coefficient sequences

Their binary sums are all h2−m, and their scaled tails before position m agree, but their scaled tails immediately after m are r. Thus any exact label-and-decoder system recovering those latter tails must have at least h+1=⌊(m+1)/2⌋+1 labels. A state determined only by the common preceding history, with no new input, cannot distinguish them. The unrestricted higher bits of the input coefficients may be chosen separately at each step, as in Proposition 10.4, so these fixed-precision symbols alone do not exclude a completion in that specified family. This says nothing about extra constraints imposed by divisor counts from one common support.

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#record:257bm-i13

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:factorial-twopow-support
Factorial-support and 2k-support instances

For every integer b≥2, both

∑k≥01b(k+1)!−1and∑k≥01b2k−1

are irrational. These are instances of the preceding theorem. For the factorial support the preceding least common multiple is k! when k≥1, so the gap is kk!. For the powers of two it is 2k−1, so the gap is 2k−1. Both tend to infinity. The conclusion concerns these two supports, not every infinite support.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:fatal-absorbing

Infinitely many greedy skips force
membership
Fix x≥0. If rn(x)>Rn at some rank n, every later rank is selected and rn+k(x)>Rn+k for every k≥0. Consequently, infinitely many omitted positive ranks imply x∈𝒜.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:final-middle-cell

Excluding minus three at a final middle
transition

Suppose that row D≥13 is a middle transition in Theorem 5.16 and every transition at a row s≥D+1 is right. Then

CD:=4rem(D)−pD−−4≠−3.

This excludes one particular value under the stated tail assumption; it neither excludes every final middle transition nor proves the all-middle-row hypothesis of Theorem 6.9.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:frozen-margin

Equivalent sign and vanishing
conditions

For the prefix D=G∩{1,…,k} define

Fk(J)=∑i=1JcD(k+1+i)2J−i−2JCD(k).

This is a finite integer expression: it compares the next J divisor counts of the fixed prefix with its centred carry. Let sn denote the integer greedy remainder at depth 2n, with weights q(2n,d) for 2≤d<n and target 22n−1−2n. The following conditions each imply 1/2∈𝒜:

  1. For every skipped rank n≥3, Fn−1(n)≥0.

  2. For every skipped rank n≥3 at which the real and integer greedy words agree on {2,…,n−1}, sn=0.

  3. For every skipped rank n≥3, B(2n)<sn.

Conditions (i) and (ii) are equivalent. Condition (iii) implies them; no converse or strict separation is established here. These hypotheses must hold at every indicated skipped rank, not merely through a finite computed range.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:full-support
Full-support irrationality, unconditional, every base b≥2

For every integer b≥2,

∑k=0∞1bk+1−1is irrational.

Hypotheses: b∈ℕ, b≥2. Conclusion: unconditional irrationality of the full-support Erdős–Borwein-type series at every base, not merely base 2. The base-2 instance recovering the classical Erdős–Borwein constant’s irrationality is a one-line corollary.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:full-support-catalogue

Erdős–Borwein full-support
irrationality, unconditional

For every integer b≥2, the sum ∑n≥1(bn−1)−1 is irrational. This is Erdős’s theorem [1]; at base 2 the sum is the Erdős–Borwein constant. The result concerns full support, not all its infinite subsets.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:geometry
Achievement-set geometry

𝒜 is compact, closed, perfect, totally disconnected and nowhere dense, and volume⁡(𝒜)=1. Thus its measure is positive although it contains no interval. Its convex hull is [0,E], where E=∑n≥1wn. The positive-index digit coding onto 𝒜 is injective: each achievable real has exactly one support.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:greedy-survival

Membership equals greedy survival; the
fatal-gap dichotomy

For a real target x≥0, let rn(x) be the remainder after the greedy rule has processed weights w1,…,wn, and let Rn=∑j>nwj, with r0(x)=x and R0=E. Then

x∈𝒜⟺x≥0  and  rn(x)≤Rn for every n≥0.

For every x∈[0,E], nonmembership is equivalent to a finite strict gap between the two next-prefix intervals; see Observation obs:general-target-gap.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:greedy-survival-catalogue
Greedy survival and membership

With the greedy remainder rn(x) and complete tail Rn,

x∈𝒜⟺x≥0 and rn(x)≤Rn for every n≥0.

If all inequalities hold, the nonnegative remainders tend to zero because Rn→0, so the greedy partial sums converge to x. Conversely, strict tail domination wn>Rn forces the greedy choices in any representation and therefore gives every inequality. The argument applies to positive summable weights satisfying that separation hypothesis; it is not a consequence of summability alone.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:greedy-survival-record

Membership equals greedy survival at
every level

For a real x, let rn(x) be its greedy remainder after rank n, and let Rn=∑j>nwj, as in the initial notation. Then

x∈𝒜⟺x≥0 and rn(x)≤Rn for every n≥0.

The inequality says that the unselected tail has enough total mass at every rank. A failure at any one rank excludes membership; the inequalities at all ranks give a representation.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:half-skip-dichotomy

The half-skip dichotomy via
Erdős–Borwein irrationality

The half target satisfies

12∈𝒜⟺ℕ>0∖G is infinite,

where G is the greedy support for 1/2. In the forward direction, finitely many skipped exponents would express the full Mersenne sum as 1/2 plus a finite rational sum, contradicting Erdős’s full-support irrationality theorem. The reverse implication uses the greedy tail criterion: once a remainder exceeds the whole available tail, every later exponent is selected. Infinitely many skips exclude that failure. The equivalence does not establish that infinitely many skips actually occur.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:largest-skip-late

Keeping the largest skipped rank beyond
two thirds

Let Ds⊆{2,…,s−1} be the support of the integer-greedy row defined in Section 5.4. Assume the following implication for every s≥14 and every largest omitted rank d=max({2,…,s−1}∖Ds):

2s<3d⟹2(s+1)<3dors∉Ds+1.

Then 1/2∈𝒜. The hypothesis says that either the same omitted rank remains beyond two thirds of the next row, or the next row omits its terminal rank. The latter alternative is exactly an upper or middle transition in the preceding classification.

The cited finite calculation establishes the initial inequality at row 14. The displayed implication then preserves the inequality by induction and supplies omitted ranks tending to infinity. It is an unproved condition on every later row; the verified base case alone does not establish it.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:last-skip-iff-fatal

Last-skip iff local fatality: a
pointwise criterion

Keep G for the selected half-greedy support, rM(1/2) for its remainder and RM for the complete tail after rank M. A positive rank M is the last omitted rank if and only if M∉G and rM(1/2)>RM. Consequently,

12∈𝒜⟺rM(1/2)≤RMfor every positive M∉G.

Thus it suffices to check the tail inequality at the ranks actually omitted by the greedy rule. This is an equivalence on that fixed orbit; it does not establish the inequality at its unboundedly many possible omitted ranks.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:lcm-gap-engine

Irrationality from a gap beyond the
preceding least common multiple

For an integer base b≥2 and strictly increasing support a:ℕ→ℕ with a(0)≥1: if a(k)−lcm(a(0),…,a(k−1))→∞, then ∑k′1/(ba(k)−1) is irrational. The base may vary over the integers, but the denominators remain ba(k)−1. Applying the argument to another denominator sequence would require its own divisibility and tail estimates.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:lower-bound-every-reset

A: a sufficient lower bound at every
reset

Assume that |rem(r+1)−2r+1|>2(r+5)/2 for every upper or middle reset r≥10. Then 1/2∈𝒜.

Here is the role of the constants. Put

B(r)=2⌊(r+4)/2⌋+2r+3.

For r≥10, one has B(r)2≤2r+5. A right branch at the first crossing of the largest omitted rank r would force |Δr+1|≤B(r), by tracing the exact affine recurrence back to that reset. The assumed strict lower bound excludes this crossing. The largest-skip induction then gives half-membership. The hypothesis concerns every actual reset beyond the threshold; neither a long finite check nor an asserted run-length asymptotic supplies it.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:master-dichotomy

Nonmembership of one half and a finite
fatal gap

The value 1/2 is not in 𝒜 if and only if there are an integer d≥0 and a finite set u⊆{1,…,d} such that

Xu(2)+Rd+1<12<Xu(2)+wd+1.

One implication is Lemma 6.37. For the other, follow the greedy prefixes: nonmembership forces a first failure of the tail inequality, hence one of these gaps. The endpoint equalities are excluded by Lemma 6.38.

A finite prefix and strict gap provide a nonmembership witness. The tail inequality can be certified by rational truncation bounds as in Theorem 2.11. Membership, in contrast, asserts that no such witness exists; failure to find one in a finite search is not a proof. The reduction uses wn>Rn, not compactness alone. The totient weights fail this hypothesis, as the example after Lemma 6.34 shows.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:master-identity
Decomposition of the integer remainder

For every quotient row n≥6,

(I)Δn=K(2n)+∑d∈Skipn⌊4n2d−1⌋.

Here the take and skip sets, capacity and remainder are those defined at the start of this subsection. The identity separates the contribution of the full exponent range from that of the omitted ranks. It makes no claim that there are few omitted ranks; controlling their sum is a separate part of any application.
Proof. For d=n the quotient is 2n+1, and for n<d≤2n it is 22n−d. Hence

∑d=n2n⌊4n2d−1⌋=2n+1+∑j=0n−12j=2n+1.

Substitute this in the definition of K(2n), split {2,…,n−1}=Dn⊔Skipn, and use Δn=22n−1−2n+1−∑d∈Dnw(n,d). This gives (I). Certification: rows 6≤n≤200 rechecked with zero mismatches by an exact program (§5.7).
Use: (I) permits substitution of information about K(2n). A resulting estimate for Δn must also retain or bound the skip-set sum; information about K alone need not control their cancellation.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:mersenne-channel-growth

Exponential growth of the reduced
denominators

For an integer t≥5, put

Ht=lcm⁡(1,…,t),rt=∏p≤tp,ht=Ht/rt,Dt=den⁡(htB(rt)),

where the product is over primes. Then Dt≥2t/2. Its exact denominator is

Dt=2rt−1gcd(2rt−1,htArt).
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:mersenne-channel-survival
Denominators of finite Mersenne sums

Let t≥1 and h≥1 be integers, and let r≥1 be squarefree with every prime factor at most t. Let P be a set of prime divisors of r such that t<2p for each p∈P, and put C=∏p∈P(2p−1). Then

Cgcd(C,h) | den⁡(hB(r)).

In particular, C divides this reduced denominator when gcd(C,h)=1. The factors in C are pairwise coprime, since gcd(2p−1,2q−1)=2gcd(p,q)−1=1 for distinct primes. The assertion concerns this finite signed sum; it does not replace the approximation hypotheses in Theorem 6.14.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:middle-allright-defect

The tail inequality at a final middle
transition

Suppose row D≥13 is middle and all rows after it are right. Let FD=DD∪{D} and put

CD=4rem(D)−pD−−4,ΘD=∑j≥1cFD(2D+2+j)2−j.

Then CD<ΘD. Since 0≤ΘD≤|FD|, an estimate in the opposite direction would exclude this scenario. No such reverse estimate is assumed or proved here. Remark 10.8 states the corresponding sufficient hypothesis with the value −3 excepted.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:middle-producer-escape

Two sufficient bounds at middle
transitions

Suppose that at every middle transition with row s≥13,

|Ds|+ps−+5<4rem(s).

Then 1/2∈𝒜. The stronger condition rem(s)≥s at all such rows also suffices.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:mobius-centred-nonneg
Möbius-centred carry nonnegativity below 1/2

If 1∉A and XA(2)<1/2, then CA(N)≥0 for every N. Indeed,

ihc⁡(A,N)=2N+1(1/2−XA(2))+∑j>N+1cA(j)2N+1−j>0.

The carry is an integer, so it is at least 1; subtracting 1 gives the asserted nonnegativity of the centred carry. The strict inequality and integrality are both needed in this argument. The statement is about the divisor counts cA, not a new irrationality criterion.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:mobius-lambert-identity

The Lambert-series identity for the
Möbius function

The absolutely convergent signed series satisfies

∑d≥1μ(d)2d−1=12.

This classical identity is also recorded in [7]. Expand each denominator geometrically and interchange the absolutely convergent sums. The coefficient of 2−n is ∑d∣nμ(d), equal to 1 for n=1 and 0 otherwise. This proves the identity. Its coefficients are −1,0,1, not indicators of a support; the identity therefore does not represent 1/2 as a subseries with all coefficients in {0,1}.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:multiples-support

Multiples-support irrationality via
dilation

For integers b≥2 and d≥1,

Xdℕ>0(b)=∑k≥11(bd)k−1

is irrational. This is the full-support result (Theorem 6.14) at the integer base bd; no new support argument is required.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:nine-way-hub

Equivalent descriptions of
half-membership

Each of the following is equivalent to 1/2∈𝒜:

  1. The integer-greedy sequence is not eventually always on branch R.

  2. There are arbitrarily large s≥5 with s∉Ds+1.

  3. Upper or middle transitions occur at arbitrarily large rows.

  4. Some sequence sj→∞ satisfies sj∉Dsj+1 for every j.

  5. There are rows sj→∞ and omitted ranks dj∈{2,…,sj−1}∖Dsj with dj→∞.

  6. The positive ranks omitted by the real half-greedy rule form an infinite set.

  7. The real half-greedy rule has no last omitted positive rank.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:odd-support
Odd support
For every integer b≥2, the series ∑n≥1, n odd(bn−1)−1 is irrational. This density-1/2 support is the case treated explicitly by Luca and Tachiya [3].
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:one-sided
One-sidedness

Non-membership of 1/2 in 𝒜 has an effectively checkable finite-certificate formulation, hence a Σ10 formulation. Membership has the complementary Π10 formulation. Survival through a tested finite depth alone does not establish membership; a uniform theorem or inductive invariant could. The arithmetical-hierarchy form by itself proves neither undecidability nor the absence of finite proofs.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:one-sided-finite-decision-boundary

C: the one-sided finite decision
boundary

The equivalence of Theorem 5.10 separates two logically different kinds of evidence. A fatal greedy gap found at a finite rank is a finite certificate that 1/2∉𝒜. By contrast, membership requires survival at every rank; this paper supplies no finite certificate that the orbit survives forever and no completion theorem turning a long surviving prefix into membership.

The reset-crossing hypotheses, truncation-rung ladder, and sharp-capacity inequalities feed sufficient conditions for membership. They are not proved equivalent to one another, nor is failure to find one at a given depth evidence of survival. Consequently these searches give at most a semi-decision procedure for nonmembership of the specific value 1/2. Halting does not prove the universal statement in #257, and non-halting does not prove that 1/2 is represented. In particular, neither truth nor falsity of the universal problem is shown semi-decidable here. Deeper negative search alone establishes nothing beyond the tested finite ranks; this is the quantifier boundary of Theorem 2.11.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:pairwise-coprime

Pairwise-coprime support irrationality,
Erdős 1968
For every integer b≥2 and every infinite pairwise-coprime support A⊆ℕ>0 with summable reciprocals, ∑a∈A1/(ba−1) is irrational.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:periodic-support
Periodic-support irrationality

Let b≥2 and m≥1 be integers. Suppose A⊆ℕ>0 is nonempty and satisfies n∈A if and only if n+m∈A for every n≥1. Then XA(b) is irrational.

The indicator of A is a nonzero purely periodic integer weight, so this follows from Luca and Tachiya’s theorem stated above. The linked declaration supplies a separate formal proof. At m=1 the only nonempty periodic support is full support; residue classes and unions of residue classes give the other immediate examples.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:perturbed-family-maximality

Perturbed-family maximality and the
three-branch recurrence

Use the family and adjacent pair of Definition 6.61, and assume in addition that B<g. At capacity C′=4C+g, the largest admissible updated value is t(x+) if 4o+p+≤g, and t(x−) otherwise. After this choice, apply the take-if-possible rule to an additional weight W=2g+4. The resulting remainder is

{g−4o−p+,4o+p+≤g,4r+g−p−,4o+p+>g and 4r+g−p−<W,4r−g−p−−4,4o+p+>g and 4r+g−p−≥W.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:purely-periodic-support
Purely periodic support

For integers b≥2 and m≥1, and every m-periodic A⊆ℕ (i.e. n+m∈A⇔n∈A for all n) containing a positive element, the support series ∑a∈A, a≥1(ba−1)−1 is irrational. Hypotheses: b≥2, m≥1, A m-periodic, ∃a>0, a∈A.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:real-form

Real (non-integer) form of the quotient
identity

Let xd:=1/(2d−1) and define the constant

C:=∑d≥2xd−12=E−32=0.1066951524152917…,

where E is the Erdős–Borwein constant. Then, for every quotient row n≥6,

(II)Δn=4n(∑d∈Skipnxd−C)+ηn,|ηn|<2n+2.

Proof. Splitting the full series at n gives

ηn=4nRn−1−2n+1+∑d∈Dn{4n2d−1}.

The tail bounds 2−(n−1)<Rn−1≤2−(n−1)+234−(n−1) and |Dn|≤n−2 show 0<ηn<n+2/3<2n+2.

Use of the error bound. For H>2n+2, the condition |∑d∈Skipnxd−C|>(H+2n+2)/4n is sufficient for |Δn|>H. Conversely, |Δn|>H implies |∑d∈Skipnxd−C|>(H−2n−2)/4n. Thus a square-root-exponential deviation corresponds to a separation of order 2−3n/2, with the displayed additive error retained. This is not an exact equivalence after simply discarding that error.
Note: C=E−3/2 is Mersenne-specific, but the shape “scaled deviation = 4n⋅(finite skip-sum − target constant) +O(n)” is a template, not yet matched to any analogous constant on the #249 side.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:residue-class-support
Residue-class support
For integers b≥2, m≥1 and c, the series ∑n≥1, n≡c(modm)(bn−1)−1 is irrational.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:residue-odd

Residue-class and odd-support
irrationality
For integers b≥2, m≥1 and a residue c, ∑n≥1n≡c(modm)(bn−1)−1 is irrational. Specializing m=2,c=1: ∑n odd1/(bn−1) is irrational for every b≥2, the case treated explicitly in [3].
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:seam-limit

The quotient remainders converge to the
greedy deficit

Let G be the real greedy support for 1/2, and let Ds be the integer-greedy support at row s. Then

XDs(2)⟶XG(2),rem(s)4s⟶δ:=12−XG(2)≥0.

In particular, the following conditions are equivalent: 1/2∈𝒜; the full sequence rem(s)/4s tends to zero; and there exist sj→∞ with rem(sj)/4sj→0.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:second-channel

Second-channel phase separation
sufficiency

Define Pn=4n(2rn(1/2)−2−n). If

16+37562−n≤|Pn−13|for every n≥1,

then 1/2∈𝒜. These are exact rational inequalities because the target and every finite greedy remainder are rational. The cited finite calculation establishes them for 1≤n≤6; it therefore suffices to prove them for every n≥7.

Unlike Theorem 6.3, this hypothesis concerns every positive rank, not only skipped ranks. It excludes an explicit interval around 1/3. For example, Pn∉(0,1) implies the displayed inequality when n≥2, but no such avoidance theorem for the whole orbit is proved here.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:sharp-fatal-gap

A weaker sufficient test against the
remaining tail

Let k,u,L be positive integers, and put a=2L−(2k−1)u. Suppose a>0, equivalently that ρ=u/(2L)<wk and the greedy rule skips weight wk. The dyadic sufficient test ρ≤2−k is equivalent to u≤a. The weaker sufficient condition

2u≤3a

ensures ρ<Rk, by comparison with 2−k+(3⋅4k)−1+(7⋅8k)−1<Rk. This conclusion excludes a fatal tail-mass deficit at the current step; it does not assert that ρ is representable by the remaining weights, or that all future greedy steps survive.

The containment of these sufficient conditions is strict even for valid rational data: (k,u,L,a)=(2,7,13,5) gives 1/4<7/26<R2. In contrast, the scalar pair (u,a)=(3,2) in the linked inequality lemma does not arise from integral L under the present parity relation. Unit numerators are nonfatal at such a skipped step, since then a≥1. Conversely, a fatal step requires 3a<2u, hence u≥2, or u≥3 when u is odd.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:signed-periodic

A formal dichotomy for signed periodic
weights

Let b≥2 and m≥1 be integers, and let w:ℕ>0→ℤ be m-periodic. Put

x=∑a≥1w(a)ba−1,cw(n)=∑d∣nw(d).

The cited formal argument gives the dichotomy that x is irrational or bkx∈ℤ for some integer k≥0. It excludes the latter alternative if cw has one sign throughout and is nonzero at arbitrarily large indices. These sign assumptions concern cw, not w. As noted above, Luca and Tachiya’s theorem already excludes the terminating alternative for every nonzero periodic w, without either sign restriction. The zero weight gives x=0.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:sqrt-bound-route

A square-root bound on the greedy
carry

For the greedy support G=G1/2, the centred carry is nonnegative. If in addition

CG(N)≤2N+4for every N≥0,

then G has infinitely many skipped indices and XG(2)=1/2. The unresolved part is the upper bound along this particular orbit. The carry identity explains its strength: a positive gap 1/2−XG(2) would contribute a term of order 2N, which cannot satisfy a square-root bound. This is distinct from the reset-deviation hypothesis of Theorem 6.10; no equivalence between the two hypotheses is asserted.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:straddle-closed-set
Straddle-prefix closed-set criterion

Suppose that for every d≥0 there is a finite support Dd⊆{1,…,d} such that

XDd(2)≤t≤XDd(2)+Rd.

Then t∈𝒜. The supports need not agree at different depths: compactness, together with Rd→0, supplies a limiting support. Conversely, truncating a support representing t supplies such finite supports. Thus this condition is an exact finite-approximation formulation of membership, not a criterion already known to hold for an unresolved target.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:supported-dichotomy
Support-restricted refinement

Use zero-based indices in this statement: coordinate j∈ℕ carries weight wj+1. For J⊆ℕ, consider the sums that use only coordinates in J. If ℕ∖J is finite, this achievement set has measure 2−|ℕ∖J|; if infinitely many coordinates are omitted, its measure is zero. Injectivity survives every restriction; perfectness is proved when J is infinite. No perfectness claim is made for finite J, whose coding range is finite.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:tempered-orbit-rigidity

Uniqueness of an integer recurrence with
a vanishing scaled limit

For any nonnegative-integer coefficient sequence c:ℕ→ℕ with c(n)≤n: the binary coefficient series Xc=∑n≥1′c(n)/2n is rational iff there exists a positive integer multiplier v and an integer orbit u:ℕ→ℤ satisfying the exact carry recurrence u(N+1)=2u(N)−v⋅c(N+1) together with the condition u(N)/2N→0. Every integer sequence satisfying both conditions obeys u(N)=v⋅Tc(N) exactly, where Tc(N)=∑j≥1c(N+j)/2j is the scaled tail. For each fixed v there is at most one such sequence. Positivity of the orbit alone is deliberately not used as an equivalent criterion: a homogeneous 2N-scaled perturbation can be added to any orbit without breaking the recurrence, so the limit condition cannot be dropped. The choices c=cA for Problem 257 and c=φ for Problem 249 both satisfy 0≤c(n)≤n. The telescoping argument is given again, with an example, in Theorem 6.105.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:topology
Achievement-set topology and measure

𝒜 (Definition 5.2) is compact, closed, perfect, totally disconnected, and nowhere dense; its Lebesgue measure is exactly 1: volume⁡(𝒜)=1. Hypotheses: none. Conclusion: 𝒜 is a Cantor set of positive measure, often called a fat Cantor set. Its measure is 1, not the length of its ambient interval [0,E], where E≈1.6067. Strict separation and summability give the compactness, unique coding, and Cantor topology, and Hornich’s strict-tail theorem, as proved by Nitecki [4], gives the measure as limN2NRN with RN=∑n>Nxn: each level-N cylinder has length RN, and the 2N disjoint cylinders have total length 2NRN. The Mersenne-specific input is 2NRN→1. Other weight sequences require their own tail asymptotic.
Use: Theorem 5.10 below (compactness is exactly what powers every “limit of achieved points is achieved” argument used downstream, including the seam-limit route of Part 2).
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:tr-finite-decision
Finite decision procedure

Call n∈[4,LJ/2] bad if no M∈[n,2n−2] has μJ(M)≤1115, and set B(J):=max(bad∪{3}). Then HalfRung(J) holds iff the greedy orbit for 1/2 under weights wn(J) survives every rank from 2 through B(J). This is a finite exact decision procedure.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:tr-witness-exclusion
Witness exclusion

statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:two-channel-cap
Two-channel and dyadic cap sufficiency

Suppose that for every n≥0 at which the next weight is skipped,

wn+1>rn(1/2)⟹rn(1/2)≤2−(n+1)+134−(n+1).

Then 1/2∈𝒜. The stronger bound rn(1/2)≤2−(n+1) at the same skipped ranks also suffices. The first bound retains two positive geometric terms of the full tail; it is larger, and hence less restrictive, than the second. Both are sufficient tests on the specified greedy orbit. The result does not assert that either bound holds at all its skipped ranks.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:two-sided-dyadic
A conditional two-sided dyadic bound

Assume the following two conditions for every row s≥5:

M at s⟹4rem(s)−ps−−4∉{−3,−2,−1},R at s and os≤2s⟹4os+ps+≤2s+2.

Then at every row s≥5,

rem(s)≤2soros≤2s.

The first hypothesis concerns only middle transitions. The second concerns only right transitions at which the old overshoot is at most 2s. Neither condition is asserted here for the whole sequence.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:two-thirds-band

Two-thirds band: exact localisation of
post-take skip-unsafety

Write a positive residual as 1/R. A skipped rank k passes the sufficient dyadic test precisely when R≥2k. Suppose a weight at rank b is taken without exhausting the residual: with q=2b−1, assume 0<R<q. The new reciprocal residual is Rq/(q−R). If the next take is at rank c≥b+2, put m=2c−1. The last skipped rank is dyadically unsafe exactly when

m−1<Rqq−R<m,equivalentlyq(m−1)q+m−1<R<qmq+m.

Clearing the positive denominators proves the equivalence. The interval has width q2/((q+m)(q+m−1)).

For a single skipped rank, c=b+2 and m=2q+2. The width is then q2/((3q+1)(3q+2))<1/9, and the interval lies inside 2q<3R<2q+2/3. In this single-skip case, the cited corollaries exclude integral R and show that a reduced pre-take residual p/(2D) with p,D,q odd can be unsafe only if p≥7. The latter conclusion uses the divisibility by 4 of 6D−2pq under the unsafe-band inequalities.

These are local transition statements, not bounds on the actual half-greedy orbit. Dyadic safety is only sufficient for the current tail test. The odd-coprime data (p,D,b)=(17,41,3) give an unsafe single-skip example; no conclusion that the half-greedy orbit avoids such data follows from the band calculation.
statement:erdos257-mersenne-reasoning-surface#thm:upper-reset-band
Upper-reset dyadic-band escape, checked for 13≤d≤30

The upper-reset dyadic-band escape condition requires the following at every actual upper reset d≥13: for every 0≤j≤d, the reset charge avoids a linear-width band immediately below the dyadic power 2d−j+1 (2d−j+1<resetCharge or resetCharge+2(d+j)≤2d−j+1). Granted this, 1/2∈𝒜. The linked proof verifies this condition for 13≤d≤30, using exact successor remainders at rows 14–31 (for example, rem(14)=392 and rem(31)=4187487147). This finite verification does not supply the hypothesis for every d≥13.
